records.name: Kelantan
records.summary:
In August 2026 the Kelantan assembly passed a new Syariah Criminal Offences Bill — including a clause making gender change an offence for persons under the state's syariah jurisdiction — replacing provisions of the state's 2019 syariah criminal code that Malaysia's Federal Court had struck down as outside state power. The Bill also carries "protection of modesty" decency offences, backed by whipping (3–6 strokes), fines up to RM5,000 and imprisonment up to three years.

The sequence — invalidation by the federal courts, prompt deliberate re-enactment by the state assembly — documents institutional determination to criminalise gender transition, not a stray provision. The gender-change offence binds Muslims, including Muslim travellers exposed to syariah proceedings; the official climate it signals reaches all trans visitors.

records.name: Terengganu
records.summary:
In May 2025 the Kuala Terengganu authority erected anti-homosexuality warning signboards at several locations, including near youth-frequented areas around a state university; when criticised, a state executive councillor publicly confirmed the installations were deliberate, framing them as a "constant reminder" to steer people away from homosexuality. A prominent transgender activist and, on 14 May 2025, thirteen civil-society organisations led by a national trans-rights group demanded removal, calling the boards discriminatory hate speech.

The state also retains hudud-style penal provisions (2002) that remain inoperative because a federal statute caps the sentences state religious courts may impose — confirmed current in a 2026 review — while discretionary syariah offences and the federal criminal prohibition of same-sex conduct do apply. What visitors meet here is open, ongoing official hostility, without any trans-status-specific criminalisation documented in the surviving sources.

freshness.fact: Legal analysis still sound: Terengganu's 2002 hudud-qisas provisions remain unenforceable under the federal Act 355 ceiling, while state syariah uqub offences and federal s377 stand. Post-2023 state PAS crackdown rhetoric found only via secondary reports.

records.name: Kedah
records.summary:
In October 2020 a private birthday party was raided and 30 transgender women were singled out from the gathering and arrested, while the event's organiser was separately investigated for "encouraging vice". A coalition of Malaysian human-rights organisations publicly protested, identifying a pattern of punishing organisers and allies of trans people rather than only trans people themselves.

The raid's design — isolating trans women as a category from a mixed party — evidences enforcement capacity and willingness aimed at transgender people specifically. The surviving sources date from 2020 and document no later Kedah-specific incident series.

records.name: West Java
records.summary: The most concentrated wave of mob violence against transgender women in Indonesia: ten attacks on 45 victim-survivors in Bogor between 30 March and 15 July 2026, documented by Pelangi Nusantara — groups of 10–20 men punched, kicked, threw stones, glass bottles and firecrackers at trans women and stripped some of them naked, filming the assaults for social media under the account @bogorbersihlgbt ('Bogor clean of LGBT'). No alleged perpetrator has been publicly identified, arrested or prosecuted; a trans-rights activist who accompanied women filing police reports said officers 'accepted the case but worked on it half-heartedly,' and some survivors were too afraid to report. Separately, on 22 June 2025 police detained 75 people at a villa raid in the Puncak area of Bogor Regency at a gathering labelled a 'gay party' that violated no law — Amnesty demanded their release. Activists attribute the violence's legitimisation to Perpres 111/2025, which from October 2025 lists 'LGBTQ culture' as a national-resilience threat alongside terrorism and drug abuse: 'people feel able to commit violence arbitrarily because they believe the state has legitimised that violence.' The pattern-plus-impunity combination is West Java-specific; national same-sex criminalisation does not by itself explain the street-vigilante wave with total state inaction and explicit anti-trans branding over four months.

records.name: West Sumatra
records.summary:
The clearest enacted modern local anti-LGBT bylaw outside Aceh: Bukittinggi City Regional Regulation (Perda) No. 2 of 2024 on public order, articles 43-44, prescribes oral and written warnings, cessation of activities, social rehabilitation programmes, and administrative fines of Rp1,000,000 targeting LGBT people. Enforcement is real but contested: a 2026 field study of the Perda's implementation reports supervision, enforcement and guidance by the local order force (Satpol PP), with sanctions of suboptimal effectiveness and rehabilitation hampered because the facilities barely exist; a 2025 study records people recorded as swept up in LGBT sweeps/app findings jumping from 56 in 2023 to 272 in 2024, and customary-law actors pushing parallel measures (a boarding-house barcode system, proposed nagari regulations on social deviance). Limapuluh Kota regency finalised a draft (ranperda, articles 13-14) on public tranquility containing an explicit LGBT prohibition with administrative fines in the tens of millions of rupiah plus mandated "rehabilitation" (psychosocial counselling, spiritual guidance, resocialisation) for people of same-sex attraction. OutRight's Creeping Criminalisation mapping of discriminatory regional regulations covers eight other provinces (not West Sumatra itself, whose key bylaws postdate the study), but documents the same regional-autonomy mechanism this province's bylaws instantiate.

This sits below the national score because an enacted bylaw with specified sanctions creates visitor-facing risk (detention, forced rehabilitation programmes, fines)

records.name: Bali
records.summary:
Bali is Indonesia's most tolerant mainstream environment: 2026 travel guidance still describes a "live and let live" ethos, with gay-friendly life concentrated in Seminyak, Canggu and Ubud, and no criminal enforcement against foreign tourists recorded. That informality, however, is not protection. The national penal code brought into force in 2026 criminalises extramarital sex, including same-sex relations; LGBTQ+ travel advisories rate the island "Exercise Significant Caution", public displays of affection are discouraged for all couples, and same-sex marriage remains unrecognised.

A 2025 ethnographic study of the island's trans women (transpuan) communities pointedly challenges the "refuge" framing, documenting persistent misrecognition and systemic discrimination beneath the tolerant surface. Visitors should read Bali as relatively safer by local custom — with the new penal code, conservative local administration and documented structural discrimination setting the limits of that safety.

records.name: Papua
records.summary:
No trans-specific legal measure or incident series is documented for this province in the surviving sources. The security environment, however, is not neutral: rights monitors recorded 138 acts of torture or ill-treatment in detention by police and military in the highland conflict zones of the island's western half between September 2021 and early 2025, "with almost no consequences", and a further surge of military deployments, fatal shootings and arbitrary detentions from August 2025, alongside internal displacement.

For any visitor — including a transgender one — contact with security forces in the highland districts carries a documented risk of arbitrary detention and mistreatment, and the surveillance environment raises the chance of being noticed and questioned. This is a general-population security finding, not evidence of trans-specific targeting.

records.name: South Sulawesi
records.summary:
In April 2025 Makassar's mayor Munafri 'Appi' Arifuddin reaffirmed his commitment to pushing through an anti-LGBT Perda after a same-sex act at a night entertainment venue went viral; the deputy chair of the DPRD's legislation body, Anwar Faruq, backed it as urgently needed "to preserve moral order and religious norms." South Sulawesi is one of the eight provinces analysed in OutRight International's discriminatory-regulation mapping. No enacted local bylaw with specified penalties yet exists in the province, and no violence wave or mass police raid against trans people is documented in the dossier.

The small negative deviation from the national score reflects an active legislative push in a major domestic-tourism gateway to eastern Indonesia, raising the probability of future discriminatory enforcement. It remains above West Sumatra (0.11), where a Perda with articles specifying fines and rehabilitation is already on the books, and above Jakarta (0.12), where a 56-person raid without legal basis has already occurred: the law here is proposed, not enacted, and per the enforcement-over-statute rule the traveler-facing impact is prospective.
